note: Analyst layer for the Maritime risk page. Edit this file to update outlooks, premiums and incidents. Chokepoint names, threat levels, summaries and issues come from data/risk.json so the two pages stay in step.

zones.name: Persian Gulf, Hormuz and Gulf of Oman
Bab el-Mandeb and Gulf of Aden

extra_chokepoints.s: The long way round Africa, now carrying much of the Asia–Europe traffic that avoids the Red Sea.
i: Ships avoiding Bab el-Mandeb and Suez add roughly 10 to 14 days on Asia–North Europe voyages by sailing round the Cape.
Winter storms off South Africa slow ships and raise the risk of lost containers.
Extra demand for fuel and repairs strains South African ports.

strait-of-hormuz.baseline_label: the four months before the war

scenarios: Stays near-closed
Sporadic transits on Iran’s preferred route or under escort, with attacks continuing.
Partial reopening
A US–Iran arrangement via Qatar allows escorted or licensed transits; mine risk keeps volumes low.
Wider escalation
Mining or strikes on Gulf ports and terminals push traffic close to zero.
outlook.why: Talks are live through Qatar, but Iran has set seven conditions and Washington says it does not need a deal. Attacks have continued every few days into November.

strait-of-hormuz.resolution: Weeks to months. Even after a deal, insurers and owners would wait for mine clearance and a run of incident-free transits before returning in volume.
expect: War cover is written for seven days and re-rated every 24 hours, so quotes can move sharply between booking and transit.
Crews can refuse to sail into areas designated as warlike operations zones.
GPS jamming and spoofing are widespread, so AIS positions in the Gulf are less reliable than elsewhere.
Queues and storage build at Fujairah and Yanbu as cargoes look for bypass routes.

premium.text: 6–10% of hull value for tankers in October, against about 0.25% before the war. On a $100 million tanker that is $6–10 million for one voyage.
src: CES Intelligence, citing Marsh via Insurance Business (Oct 2026)

alt.label: Pipeline bypasses
alt.note: There is no sea route around Hormuz. Some crude can bypass it through Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea and the UAE’s Habshan–Fujairah pipeline to the Gulf of Oman, but Yanbu cargoes then face Houthi risk in the Red Sea.

strait-of-hormuz.decision: Most owners are waiting or using the pipeline bypasses. Transit only makes sense where the cargo margin covers a premium of several million dollars and the charter terms say who pays it.

bab-el-mandeb.baseline_label: January to October 2023, before Houthi attacks began
bab-el-mandeb.status: Open, but most carriers still avoid it

scenarios: Threat holds at current level
Occasional attacks and constant threat keep most container lines on the Cape route.
Escalation
Houthi strikes widen to Saudi-linked shipping and Red Sea ports as the Iran war continues.
Meaningful de-escalation
A wider Gulf settlement lets carriers start testing the route again.
outlook.why: Houthi missile and drone capability is intact and their attacks on Saudi energy sites this week show they are still escalating.

bab-el-mandeb.resolution: No near-term end. Carriers have said they need months of calm before returning, and the threat is now tied to the Iran war.
expect: Container lines keep Cape routings in their schedules, so transit times stay 10 to 14 days longer on Asia–Europe services.
Saudi-linked tankers loading at Yanbu pay far higher war cover than other Red Sea traffic.
Naval escorts are limited and do not cover every vessel.

premium.text: About 0.5% of hull value for the most exposed corridor (July), against 0.1% near western Saudi Arabia. Saudi-linked tankers at Yanbu were quoted around 3% in late September.
src: Al Jazeera, citing S&P Global (23 Jul 2026)

reroute.note: Asia–North Europe, compared with the Suez route.

alt.label: Cape of Good Hope route
alt.note: The usual alternative for Asia–Europe trade: about 3,500 nautical miles and 10 to 14 days longer than going through Suez.

bab-el-mandeb.decision: For most container and tanker trades the Cape route is still cheaper than the risk. Transit is mainly chosen by ships with little perceived link to Israel, the US or Saudi Arabia.

suez-canal.baseline_label: January to October 2023, before Houthi attacks began

scenarios: Stays depressed
Traffic follows Bab el-Mandeb: no recovery while the southern Red Sea stays dangerous.
Gradual recovery
Some carriers trial the route if the Red Sea quietens.
Further fall
Wider Red Sea escalation pushes more ships to the Cape.
outlook.why: The canal itself is safe. Its traffic depends almost entirely on security at the southern end of the Red Sea.

suez-canal.resolution: Tied to Bab el-Mandeb. Expect months rather than weeks.
expect: Egypt has offered toll discounts to win traffic back, with limited effect.
Northern Red Sea war cover is far cheaper than at Bab el-Mandeb, which helps ships serving Saudi and Jordanian ports.

premium.text: About 0.1% of hull value in the northern Red Sea near western Saudi Arabia (July), well below the Bab el-Mandeb rate.
src: Al Jazeera, citing S&P Global (23 Jul 2026)

reroute.note: Asia–North Europe, compared with the Suez route.

suez-canal.decision: The canal is only worth using if the voyage avoids the southern Red Sea or the owner accepts Bab el-Mandeb risk.

bosporus.status: Open; ships near Ukrainian and Russian ports under drone and missile threat

scenarios: Strikes continue
Both sides keep hitting ships and ports linked to the other.
Narrow calm
An energy or maritime truce from the Abu Dhabi track lowers the strike rate.
Sharp escalation
Strikes widen to neutral shipping or Turkish waters.
outlook.why: Russia says it struck three cargo ships around Odesa and Chornomorsk on 8 November, and Ukraine keeps targeting shadow-fleet tankers. Talks in Abu Dhabi produced a prisoner swap, not a ceasefire.

bosporus.resolution: Linked to the wider war. A maritime truce is possible but has not been agreed.
expect: War cover for Black Sea calls is now quoted per port and per voyage, and quotes are volatile.
Sanctioned Russian tankers transit the Bosporus, so screening counterparties matters as much as security.

premium.text: Up to 1% for some Ukrainian ports in early November, from 0.25–0.3% before the latest attacks. Exceptional quotes near 20% were reported for the CPC terminal in late October.

bosporus.decision: There is no sea alternative for Black Sea ports. The choice is whether to accept a specific port call, wait for a quieter window, or move cargo through Danube or rail links.

taiwan-strait.status: Open, normal commercial traffic under military pressure

scenarios: Steady coercion
Daily Chinese military and coast guard activity without disruption to commercial shipping.
Exercise or quarantine disruption
Large drills close areas for days and ships reroute east of Taiwan.
Blockade
A blockade or quarantine stops traffic to Taiwan’s ports.
outlook.why: Pressure is constant but calibrated. The APEC meeting in Shenzhen on 18–19 November gives Beijing a reason to avoid a crisis this month.

taiwan-strait.resolution: Not applicable while traffic is normal. Any closure from drills would likely last days.
expect: Short-notice live-fire zones can force reroutes east of Taiwan.
Any crisis would quickly bring war-risk premiums to Asian routes that have not paid them before.

premium.text: No widely reported additional war-risk premium for commercial transits.

reroute.note: Rough figure for north–south coastal routes; the detour is usually under a day.

taiwan-strait.decision: Business as usual, but voyage plans should include an east-of-Taiwan fallback and charter terms should cover sudden closures.

scenarios: Normal operations
Heavy but routine traffic, with low-level robbery in the Singapore Strait.
Local disruption
A collision, spill or robbery spike slows traffic for days.
Wider disruption
South China Sea tension spills over to onward routes.
outlook.why: No state actor threatens the strait directly. The main risks are accidents and petty crime.

expect: Robbery of anchored or slow ships in the Singapore Strait continues; ReCAAP publishes incident reports.
Larger ships that cannot use Malacca already go via Lombok.

reroute.note: Rough figure; depends on origin and destination.

alt.label: Sunda Strait detour
alt.note: The fallback if Malacca were blocked, adding roughly one to three days.

strait-of-malacca.decision: No action needed beyond normal security watchkeeping in the Singapore Strait.

scenarios: Normal operations
Water levels are adequate and transits run normally.
Political disruption
The US–China port dispute affects terminal operations at either end.
Draught limits
An early dry spell forces limits on ship size.
outlook.why: The canal is operating normally. The main open question is who runs the ports at each end.

expect: Booking slots in advance avoids queues in busy periods.
Port ownership disputes can affect terminal contracts rather than the canal itself.

danish-straits.status: Open; watch point for Russia’s shadow fleet

scenarios: Steady state
Shadow-fleet tankers keep transiting; coastal states inspect and document.
Tougher enforcement
More boarding, insurance checks or detentions of uninsured tankers.
Sabotage incident
Damage to a cable or pipeline brings new restrictions.
outlook.why: European states are tightening checks on uninsured tankers, and Russia escorts some of them.

expect: Tankers without proper insurance face inspection and possible detention.
Counterparty screening is the main risk for traders, not physical security.
danish-straits.decision: For legitimate operators, the risk is being near or dealing with sanctioned tankers. Screen counterparties and ship-to-ship partners.

cape-of-good-hope.baseline_label: January to October 2023, before Red Sea diversions

scenarios: Stays busy
Most Asia–Europe container traffic keeps sailing round Africa.
Heavier still
Red Sea escalation pushes the remaining Suez traffic to the Cape.
Traffic falls back
Carriers return to the Red Sea.
outlook.why: The Cape route depends on the Red Sea staying unsafe, which looks likely through the next month.

expect: Southern-hemisphere storms can add delays.
Bunker prices and availability in South Africa matter more for voyage costs.
cape-of-good-hope.decision: The default route for Asia–Europe trade while the Red Sea stays dangerous.

incidents.title: Tanker incident in the Strait of Hormuz
incidents.text: UKMTO reported an incident involving a tanker; damage and crew status were not yet known.

incidents.title: ADNOC vessel damaged in Gulf attack
incidents.text: A vessel operated by the UAE’s state oil company was damaged in an attack in the Gulf.

incidents.title: Russia says it struck three cargo ships near Odesa and Chornomorsk
incidents.text: Russia’s defence ministry claimed the ships carried weapons or dual-use goods; the claim is unverified.

incidents.title: Tanker on fire off Khasab; crew evacuated
incidents.text: A tanker caught fire about 8 nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman. Another outbound tanker was hit by a projectile the same day; its crew was safe.

incidents.title: US strikes a bulk carrier in the Gulf of Oman
incidents.text: Iran and the US traded strikes on commercial ships over the weekend; eight vessels had been attacked by Iran in Hormuz and the Gulf since 1 November.

incidents.title: JMIC: four attacks in Hormuz in 96 hours
incidents.text: The Joint Maritime Information Centre reported a rising attack rate in its 5 November advisory.

incidents.title: Two projectiles hit a tanker off Oman
incidents.text: UKMTO warning 195-26 reported a tanker struck off the Omani coast.

incidents.title: Tug Selat Storm and tanker Era S struck
incidents.text: Two vessels were hit in the Strait of Hormuz on the first day of November.

incidents.title: Tanker attacked off Saudi Arabia
incidents.text: UKMTO reported a tanker attacked in the upper Gulf offshore of Saudi Arabia.

incidents.title: Container ship GFS Pride sinks
incidents.text: A total loss for hull war underwriters.

incidents.title: Taiwan drives four Chinese ships from Kinmen waters
incidents.text: Taiwan’s coast guard escorted Chinese vessels out of restricted waters off Kinmen.
